claim: Nutrient uptake by roots often involves substrate-dependent regulated nutrient transporters.
source: Nutrient uptake by roots often involves substrate-dependent regulated nutrient transporters.
evidence: This is a general statement about plant biology presented in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript, but represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Boron is essential for plant growth but toxic at high concentrations.
source: boron is essential for plant growth but toxic at high concentrations.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the manuscript (Sakamoto et al., 2011-09) and represents established knowledge.

claim: In Arabidopsis thaliana, boron uptake occurs via diffusion facilitators (NIPs) and exporters (BORs).
source: In Arabidopsis thaliana, boron uptake occurs via diffusion facilitators (NIPs) and exporters (BORs), each presenting distinct polarity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1 and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Both NIPs and BORs manifest strikingly swift boron-dependent regulation despite homogenous and stable boron soil concentrations.
source: although boron soil concentrations are homogenous and stable, both transporters manifest strikingly swift boron-dependent regulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data cited in the manuscript (Takano et al., 2005; Tanaka et al., 2011; Tanaka et al., 2016) and is a central observation motivating the study.

claim: Slower regulation of boron transporters leads to physiologically detrimental oscillatory behaviour.
source: Through mathematical modelling, we demonstrate that slower regulation of these transporters leads to physiologically detrimental oscillatory behaviour.
evidence: This is demonstrated through mathematical modeling results shown in Figures 2-6.

claim: During oscillatory behaviour, cells become periodically exposed to potentially cytotoxic boron levels.
source: Cells become periodically exposed to potentially cytotoxic boron levels, and nutrient throughput to the xylem becomes hampered.
evidence: This is shown in modeling results in Figures 2, 3, and 5.

claim: Swift transporter regulation within a polarised tissue context is critical to prevent intrinsic traffic-jam like behaviour of nutrient flow.
source: We conclude that, while maintaining homeostasis, swift transporter regulation within a polarised tissue context is critical to prevent intrinsic traffic-jam like behaviour of nutrient flow.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the mathematical modeling analysis presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Most soils are either deficient or in excess of essential elements.
source: Most soils are either deficient or in excess of essential elements (Roy et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Roy et al., 2006.

claim: Boron is critical for cell wall composition.
source: Boron is one of such essential nutrients for plants, critical for cell wall composition (O'Neill et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to O'Neill et al., 2004.

claim: Borate cross-links a pectic polysaccharide, Rhamnogalacturonan II, making it indispensable for tissue growth.
source: Borate is cross-linking a pectic polysaccharide, Rhamnogalacturonan II, which makes it indispensable for tissue growth (Kobayashi et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kobayashi et al., 1996.

claim: At neutral pH, boron is mostly present in the form of boric acid.
source: At neutral pH, boron is mostly present in the form of boric acid (Woods, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Woods, 1996 and represents established chemical knowledge.

claim: BOR1 and BOR2 locate on the inwards-facing membranes of the cell.
source: In the root, BOR1 (At2g47160) and BOR2 (At3g62270) locate on the inwards-facing membranes of the cell (Takano et al., 2010; Miwa et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations (Takano et al., 2010; Miwa et al., 2013) and shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: NIP5;1 locates on the outwards-facing membranes.
source: while NIP5;1 (At4g10380) locates on the outwards-facing membranes (Takano et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation (Takano et al., 2010) and shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: Both nip5;1 and bor1, bor2 mutants present severe growth defects under low boron concentrations.
source: Indeed, both nip5;1 and bor1, bor2 mutants present severe growth defects under low boron concentrations (Noguchi et al., 1997; Takano et al., 2006-06; Miwa et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Noguchi et al., 1997; Takano et al., 2006-06; Miwa et al., 2013).

claim: High intracellular boron concentrations elicit DNA damage, growth retardation and eventually cell death.
source: While boron is required for cell wall strength and stability, too high intracellular boron concentrations elicit DNA damage, growth retardation and eventually cell death (Sakamoto et al., 2011-09).
evidence: This is supported by a citation (Sakamoto et al., 2011-09).

claim: Protein levels of NIP5;1 and BOR1, 2 drop at higher boron concentrations.
source: the protein levels of the boron transporters are regulated by boron itself, with both NIP5;1 and BOR1, 2 protein levels dropping at higher boron concentrations (Takano et al., 2005; Takano et al., 2006-06; Takano et al., 2010; Miwa et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and experimental observations.

claim: NIP5;1 protein down-regulation takes place through mRNA degradation.
source: In the case of NIP5;1 boron reduces protein levels via mRNA degradation (Tanaka et al., 2011; Tanaka et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations (Tanaka et al., 2011; Tanaka et al., 2016).

claim: BOR1, 2 down-regulation involves increased protein degradation.
source: while in the case of BOR1, 2 the mechanism involves increased protein degradation (Takano et al., 2005; Miwa et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Takano et al., 2005; Miwa et al., 2013).

claim: BOR1 degradation occurs through endocytosis, apparent 30 min after transfer from low to high boron media.
source: The BOR1 degradation occurs through endocytosis, apparent 30 min after the transfer from low to high boron media.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations cited in the manuscript.

claim: After two hours BOR1 has already mostly disappeared, suggesting that the half life of BOR1 is well below one hour.
source: After two hours BOR1 has already mostly disappeared, suggesting that the half life of BOR1 is well below one hour (Takano et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from Takano et al., 2005 and represents an inference from those data.

claim: The half life of NIP5;1 mRNA after transfer from low to high boron media is 10–15 min.
source: The half life of NIP5;1 mRNA after the transfer from low to high boron media is 10–15 min (Tanaka et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from Tanaka et al., 2011.

claim: Boron is very mobile in the soil due to being available as boric acid, which is highly water-soluble.
source: This is due to boron being available to plants as boric acid, which is highly water-soluble (solubility: 0.92 mol/L at 25°C). Consequently, boron is very mobile in the soil (Nable et al., 1997)
evidence: This is supported by a citation (Nable et al., 1997) and chemical properties of boric acid.

claim: Patchy heterogeneous boron levels throughout the soil are neither stable nor probable.
source: Consequently, boron is very mobile in the soil (Nable et al., 1997), rendering patchy heterogeneous boron levels throughout the soil neither stable nor probable.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high mobility of boron in soil.

claim: Soil adsorption plays a role in buffering fluctuations in boron concentration in soil water as a consequence of fluctuations in the water-soil ratio.
source: Keren and Bingham, 1985, analysing the effects of solution-to-soil ratio on the boron concentration in soil water, propose that soil adsorption plays a role in buffering the fluctuations in boron concentration in soil water as a consequence of fluctuations in the water-soil ratio.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Keren and Bingham, 1985.

claim: Boron concentration in the soil is robust against fluctuations in the water-to-soil ratio if soil adsorption is considered.
source: Mathematical modelling was used to predict the boron concentrations in the soil solution from the water-to-soil ratio (Keren, 1981), revealing that boron concentration in the soil is robust against fluctuations in the water-to-soil ratio if soil adsorption is considered.
evidence: This is based on mathematical modeling from Keren, 1981.

claim: Rapid fluctuations in boron concentration are unlikely, or rare events even if they could occur under very specific and unlikely conditions.
source: From these in-depth studies, the picture consolidates that rapid fluctuations in boron concentration are indeed unlikely, or rare events even if they could occur under very specific and unlikely conditions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies on soil boron dynamics.

claim: The model assumes that all the boron transporters of a cell are regulated by the cytosolic boron concentration within that respective cell.
source: Hence, our model assumes that all the boron transporters of a cell are regulated by the cytosolic boron concentration within that respective cell.
evidence: This is an explicit assumption stated in the model description, supported by experimental evidence for NIP5;1 (Tanaka et al., 2016).

claim: NIP5;1 mRNA degradation is triggered by boron-dependent ribosome stalling during the translation process.
source: In the case of NIP5;1, we recently revealed that NIP5;1 mRNA degradation is triggered by boron-dependent ribosome stalling during the translation process (Tanaka et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tanaka et al., 2016.

claim: The boron-dependent degradation of NIP5;1 was observed in an in vitro system without cell wall fraction, suggesting that the sensing mechanism depends on the cytoplasmic boron concentration.
source: The boron-dependent degradation was also observed in an in vitro system without cell wall fraction, which suggests that the sensing mechanism depends on the cytoplasmic boron concentration.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations that support the inference about the sensing mechanism.

claim: The parsimonious model accounts for general features of the observed transporters' expression patterns solely as a consequence of the relative positioning of the cells within the cell row.
source: It was therefore interesting to observe that our parsimonious model could already account for general features of the the observed transporters' expression patterns (Figure 2C,D) solely as a consequence of the relative positioning of the cells within the cell row
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing model results (Figure 2C,D) with experimental observations (Figure 1B).

claim: Oscillations in the individual cells are spatially coupled, manifested as a boron wave that propagates backwards over the tissue.
source: Kymographs make it visually clear that oscillations in the individual cells are in fact spatially coupled, manifested as a boron wave that propagates backwards over the tissue, that is, the pulse moves in the direction contrary to the nutrient flow itself.
evidence: This is demonstrated by kymographs shown in Figure 3.

claim: The traffic-jam-like phenomenon is conserved irrespective of the number of cells between the medium and the convective xylem flux.
source: Figure 3B–G shows that the phenomenon is conserved irrespective of the number of cells between the medium and the convective xylem flux.
evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling results shown in Figure 3B-G for tissues with 5-10 cells.

claim: The same traffic-jam-like phenomenon was observed even when the model contained 100 cell files.
source: The same phenomenon was still observed even when the model contained 100 cell files (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that large tissues do not prevent these effects from occurring, but rather increase its likelihood.
evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The phase diagram shows a large region in which the system becomes unstable and oscillations arise, as well as a region in which sufficient regulation swiftness ensures that the system is stable.
source: The phase-portrait that emerges (Figure 4A) shows a large region in which the system becomes unstable and oscillations arise (indicated in red), as well as a region in which sufficient regulation swiftness ensures that the system is stable and oscillations do not develop (indicated in blue).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the stability analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The parameter values derived to capture wild type dynamics of transporter regulation (point 1,1) fall into the stable regime.
source: From this combined analysis it becomes apparent that the parameter values we derived to capture wild type dynamics of transporter regulation (i.e., point 1,1) fall into the stable regime.
evidence: This is shown in the phase diagram in Figure 4A.

claim: Independent small reductions from wild type values in either NIP or BOR regulation rate can cause the tissue to experience oscillations.
source: However, independent small reductions from these values in either NIP or BOR regulation rate can cause the tissue to experience oscillations.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the phase diagram in Figure 4A.

claim: Both transporters are required to present a rapid response, and their combined swiftness is synergistic.
source: Not only does the analysis reveal that both transporters are required to present a rapid response, and that this is independent of the BOR-dependent fluxes becoming saturated, but their combined swiftness is synergistic: if one transporter is extremely fast, the other can be bit slower than what is otherwise needed.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the phase diagram analysis in Figure 4.

claim: Sufficiently rapid transport regulation is important to reduce the risk of DNA damage when considering absolute concentrations or the increase over the basal equilibrium boron concentrations.
source: We observe increasing maximum levels in boron concentration for slower regulation swiftness (Figure 5A), as well as higher fold-changes in boron concentration (Figure 5B). This suggests that sufficiently rapid transport regulation is important to reduce the risk of DNA damage when either considering absolute concentrations or the increase over the basal equilibrium boron concentrations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from modeling results shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Under conditions in which traffic jams and large-amplitude variations occur, there is a considerable reduction in total throughput through the tissue.
source: Moreover, under the conditions in which traffic jams and large-amplitude variations occur, we measured a considerable reduction in total throughput through the tissue (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling results shown in Figure 5C.

claim: When BOR saturation is considered, the detrimental effects of the instabilities that arise due to slowing down the regulatory dynamics are amplified.
source: In stark contrast, the detrimental effects of the instabilities that arise due to slowing down the regulatory dynamics are amplified when BOR saturation is considered (see details of saturation implementation in the caption of Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The peak levels during concentration fluctuations are more than twice as high as the default scenario when BOR saturation is considered.
source: The impact of the traffic jams becomes much more severe, with peak levels during the concentration fluctuations more than twice as high as the default scenario (compare Figure 2 to Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing modeling results in Figure 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Selective pressures operating on the root's capacity to absorb boron optimally and robustly could result in the system evolving to a regime of rapid regulation of transporters.
source: Taken all into consideration, we infer that selective pressures operating on the root's capacity to absorb boron optimally and robustly could result in the system evolving to a regime of rapid regulation of transporters.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results regarding physiological impacts.

claim: When transporter regulation is as swift as in wild type, a steady flow with no oscillation in the concentrations is observed in the ring model.
source: When transporter regulation is as swift as in wild type (Figure 6A), a steady flow with no oscillation in the concentrations is observed.
evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling results shown in Figure 6A.

claim: When transporter regulation swiftness is decreased to sufficiently low values in the ring model, oscillations arise after an initial period.
source: When transporter regulation swiftness is decreased to sufficiently low values as to cause unstable flows (as derived from the analysis shown in Figure 4), oscillations arise. After an initial period in which the flows seem constant, random numerical fluctuations in the simulation bring forth a rise of boron concentration in a random cell
evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling results shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: The unstable flow regime continuously self-propagates and is not triggered by boundary conditions.
source: These simulations demonstrate that the unstable flow regime — which we now can conclusively eliminate as being triggered by boundary conditions — continuously self-propagates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ring model simulations shown in Figure 6.

claim: Nuclear accumulations of NIP5;1 RNA represent sites of ongoing RNA production and degradation, rather than separate nuclear storage compartments.
source: This is consistent with the nuclear accumulations representing sites of ongoing RNA production and degradation, rather than separate nuclear storage compartments.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the smFISH observations.

claim: The average mature mRNA/pre-mRNA ratio of NIP5;1 was less than 25% of that of PP2A.
source: The average mature mRNA/pre-mRNA ratio of NIP5;1 was less than 25% of that of PP2A (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The low mature mRNA/pre-mRNA ratio of NIP5;1 indicates a high degradation rate of NIP5;1 mRNA.
source: In accordance with our interpretation of the smFISH results, this again indicates a high degradation rate of NIP5;1 mRNA.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the qRT-PCR data.

claim: NIP5;1 mRNA degradation could occur through two coordinated B-dependent processes: one where cytoplasmic degradation is triggered by ribosome stalling and another localised in the nucleus where RNA is turned over at the site of transcription.
source: Together these results suggest that mRNA degradation could occur through two coordinated B-dependent processes; one where cytoplasmic degradation is triggered by ribosome stalling and another localised in the nucleus where RNA is turned over at the site of transcription.
evidence: This is a speculative inference combining previous findings (Tanaka et al., 2016) with new smFISH data.

claim: The experimentally observed swiftness of boron transporters' boron-mediated downregulation can be understood as a necessary mechanism to maintain optimal constant xylem loading rates over time, while also avoiding DNA damage due to oscillations within cells.
source: We conclude that the experimentally observed swiftness of boron transporters' boron-mediated downregulation can be understood as a necessary mechanism to maintain optimal constant xylem loading rates over time, while also avoiding DNA damage due to oscillations within cells.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, drawn from the modeling analysis.

claim: Without substrate-mediated downregulation of the transporters, the plant would be unable to shield itself from toxic soil boron levels and be much less efficient in growing at low soil boron levels.
source: One could argue that without a substrate-mediated downregulation of the transporters there would not be the need to avoid traffic jam-like behaviour through swift regulatory dynamics in the first place. However, were the system not to present the regulation, the plant would be unable to shield itself from toxic soil boron levels (Figure 8A) and be much less efficient in growing at low soil boron levels (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling results shown in Figure 8.

claim: The requirement for swift transporter downregulation does not depend on external boron fluctuations in the medium, number of cell files composing the root tissue, possible saturable activity of the transporter itself nor the magnitude, location or strength of the xylem flow.
source: We showed that this is an intrinsic requirement, simply because boron transporters are polarly located: The requirement itself does not depend on external boron fluctuations in the medium, number of cell files composing the root tissue, possible saturable activity of the transporter itself nor the magnitude, location or strength of the xylem flow.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the various modeling analyses presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The phosphate and iron transport systems present both polar transporters as well as substrate-dependent regulation, serving as candidates for similar traffic-jam-like phenomena.
source: For example, the phosphate and iron transport systems present both polar transporters as well as substrate-dependent regulation, serving as candidates for such phenomena and dynamical constraint avoidance.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the findings to other transport systems.

claim: Polar accumulation of IRT1, a major Fe transporter for Fe uptake into roots, is regulated in an Fe-dependent manner.
source: Similar regulation is also reported for the iron (Fe) transport system, where polar accumulation of IRT1, a major Fe transporter for Fe uptake into roots, is regulated in an Fe-dependent manner (Barberon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Barberon et al., 2014.

claim: For any polarised tissue in which adaptive regulation of transport levels is necessary, intrinsic temporal constraints are expected to operate to ensure that steady state flows are maintained and large fluctuations avoided.
source: Indeed, for any polarised tissue in which adaptive regulation of transport levels is necessary we can expect to find intrinsic temporal constraints operating to ensure that steady state flows are maintained and large fluctuations avoided.
evidence: This is a generalization and speculation based on the findings of this study.

claim: Although both transporters are predicted to work synergistically and are both required to be effectively similar in regard to rapid regulation, their regulations are biologically encoded in unique ways.
source: In molecular terms, we discovered that although both transporters are predicted to work synergistically and are both required to be effectively similar in regard to rapid regulation, their regulations are biologically encoded in unique ways.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from both modeling and experimental observations.

claim: NIP5;1 constitutes a system in which production is maintained high but degradation is rapidly controlled transcriptionally, allowing for the necessarily rapid boron-dependent response.
source: We here experimentally focused on the regulatory swiftness of the bidirectional transporter NIP5;1, and found strong evidence that it constitutes a system in which production is maintained high but degradation is rapidly controlled transcriptionally, allowing for the necessarily rapid boron-dependent response.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the smFISH and qRT-PCR experiments.

claim: 72% of cells had at least one NIP5;1 intron signal.
source: We used this approach to further investigate NIP5;1 transcription and found 72% of cells with at least one NIP5;1 intron signal.
evidence: This is based on smFISH experimental data.

claim: 84% of cells had PP2A intron signals, as previously reported.
source: As expected, this was lower than the 84% previously reported for the more highly expressed gene PP2A (Duncan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on a citation to Duncan et al., 2016.

claim: The transcription of the transporters takes place throughout the entire root tissue, even for NIP5;1.
source: Although protein levels can present strong variation between cell files, the transcription of the transporters takes place throughout the entire root tissue, even for NIP5;1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GUS staining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The model uses the simplifying assumption that all cell files are intrinsically the same in respect to the potential of expressing the transporters, and variations arise solely as a consequence of the nutrient distributions.
source: We therefore use the simplifying assumption that all cell files are intrinsically the same in respect to the potential of expressing the transporters, and variations arise solely as a consequence of the nutrient distributions.
evidence: This is an explicit modeling assumption stated in the text.

claim: The modelled cells loosely map to the outermost epidermis (cell 1), the cortex (cell 2), the endodermis (cell 3), and finally to the pericycle/vasculature (cell 4).
source: The modelled cells loosely map to the outermost epidermis (cell 1), the cortex (cell 2), the endodermis (cell 3), and finally to the pericycle/vasculature (cell 4).
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the model structure.

claim: The last cell of the row is endowed with an upward convective flow, which captures the shootwards convective flow of the xylem.
source: The last cell of the row is endowed with an upward convective flow, which captures the shootwards convective flow of the xylem.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the model structure.

claim: The plasmamembrane's permeability rate for boric acid is relatively high compared to other nutrient elements, due to boric acid existing in a non-charged form under physiological pH.
source: Note that the plasmamembrane's permeability rate for boric acid is relatively high compared to other nutrient elements, due to boric acid existing in a non-charged form under physiological pH.
evidence: This is based on chemical knowledge about boric acid.

claim: In mature Arabidopsis the rate of transpiration is 0.1 g water/g FW tissue/hour at 70% humidity under daytime conditions.
source: Hosy et al., 2003 reported that in mature Arabidopsis the rate of transpiration is 0.1 g water/g FW tissue/hour at 70% humidity under daytime conditions.
evidence: This is based on a citation to Hosy et al., 2003.
